raw_case_text:
The patient is an 83 years-old, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-negative, Caucasian male, with a history of recurrent nasal bleedings since childhood, recurrent gingival bleedings, frequent cutaneous hematoma after minor traumata, which were attributed to ITP diagnosed at age 52 years, splenectomy at age 52 years for the ITP, coronary heart disease resulting in two myocardial infarctions at age 52 years, corticosteroids for ITP since age 53 years, steroid-induced diabetes mellitus since age 53 years, requiring insulin since age 78 years, arterial hypertension since years, hyperlipidemia since age 53 years, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty at age 62 years, aortocoronary bypass grafting at ages 64 and 75 years, atrial fibrillation since age 68 years, cataract surgery at ages 71 and 74 years, bilateral carotid artery stenosis requiring stent implantation at age 72 years, a 6-fold stent placing for coronary stenoses at age 75 years, bilateral hypoacusis since age 78 years requiring hearing devices bilaterally and sensori-motor polyneuropathy since age 78 years. Since age 82 years, he also noted a mild cognitive decline and non-specific visual impairment and started to use a stick for walking and a walker since two weeks prior to admission. His family history was positive for diabetes mellitus and short stature in his mother. From age 68 years until admission, he was taking phenprocoumon.
He was admitted at age 83 years because of chronic tiredness, dyspnea, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain. Blood chemical findings showed leucocytosis with a maximum value of 38.8/nL (n, 4.0-9.0/nL) on hospital day (hd) 3, thrombocytopenia with a minimum value of 4/nL (n, 150-450/nL) on hd 15 and hd 18, renal insufficiency, and elevated C-reactive protein with a maximum value of 34.7 mg/dL (n, <= 0.6 mg/dL) at hd 3 (Table 1). There were also elevated glutamate-oxalate transaminase, glutamate pyruvate transaminase, and lactate dehydrogenase (Table 1). Creatine-kinase was normal throughout hospitalization. There was slight hypocalcemia (Table 1) and elevation of ferritin to 3817 ng/mL (n, 30-400 ng/mL). Thyroid function parameters were indicative of hyperthyroidism. The HbA1c was 7.4% (n, <= 6%). X-ray of the lung revealed multiple reticulonodular infiltrates up to one cm in diameter over both lungs with predominance in the left lower lobe, a pleural effusion in the horizontal interlobar fissure, and an encapsulated effusion in the right-sided diagonal interlobar fissure. X-ray of the lung five weeks earlier had been normal. A CT-scan of the thorax showed an 11x7 cm, enhancing mass lesion in the right upper lobe with central and peripheral necrosis and multiple irregularly contoured hyperdensities over both lungs (Fig. 1). Sputum cultures grew Nocardia sp.
Clinical neurologic examination revealed slight dysarthria, dysphagia, bilateral ptosis, bilateral hypoacusis, postural tremor, left-sided dysdiadochokinesia, weakness for hip extension bilaterally (M5-), reduced tendon reflexes on the upper limbs and absent tendon reflexes on the lower limbs, diffuse wasting, stocking-type sensory disturbances bilaterally, and ataxic stance. He was able to walk with a walker. MRI of the cerebrum showed a hyperintense, enhancing lesion of 4 mm in diameter in the cranial part of the cerebellar vermis (Fig. 2). Additionally, there were small hyperintense lesions in the occipital deep white matter and subcortically bilaterally (Fig. 2). Lumbar puncture was recommended, but contraindicated due to ITP. No manifestations of nocardiosis other than in the lung and cerebrum were detected.
For ITP, the patient received prednisolone 50 mg/d until hd 9. For the general infection, he initially received amoxicillin between hd 2 and hd 4. From hd 4 to hd 7, he received caspofungin and between hd 5 and hd 7 piperazillin. Meropenem was started on hd 8 and maintained until hd 45. He had never developed fever during the entire hospitalization. After dismissal, the patient was switched to a long-term therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazol. Shortly after admission, oral anticoagulation was stopped because of severe thrombocytopenia of 4,000/nL (Table 1). Since hd 23, corticosteroids had to be restarted because of deteriorating ITP (Table 1). His therapy at dismissal included danazol, furosemide, pantoprazole, atorvastatin, metoprolol, enalapril, amiodarone, prednisolone, folic acid, and insulin in addition to the antibiotic. At the three month follow-up, dimension of the pulmonary lesions had regressed. On the contrary, the cerebral lesions had progressed despite trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazol, promting a switch to sultamicillin and then to meropenem. Unexpectedly, the patient died from acute myocardial infarction shortly thereafter. Autopsy excluded a pulmonary malignancy as the underlying cause of nocardiosis and confirmed that antibiotic therapy was not effective in eradicating the cerebral infection, although cerebral tissue cultures were negative for Nocardia sp.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old Caucasian male with chronic immune thrombocytopenia on long-term corticosteroids presented with chronic fatigue, dyspnea, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted with chronic tiredness, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain, having also noticed progressive gait instability requiring a walking stick and a walker over the preceding 2 weeks. He remained afebrile throughout hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-negative Caucasian male with childhood epistaxis/gingival bleeding and cutaneous hematomas diagnosed as immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) at age 52, status post splenectomy at age 52, on chronic corticosteroids since age 53; steroid-induced diabetes mellitus since age 53 (insulin-dependent since age 78); two myocardial infarctions at age 52, PTCA at age 62, CABG at ages 64 and 75, and 6-vessel coronary stenting at age 75; arterial hypertension and hyperlipidemia since age 53; atrial fibrillation on phenprocoumon since age 68; cataract surgeries at ages 71 and 74; bilateral carotid artery stenting at age 72; bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and sensorimotor polyneuropathy since age 78; mild cognitive decline and visual impairment since age 82. Maternal family history of diabetes mellitus and short stature.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications included phenprocoumon, corticosteroids, and insulin.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile. Neurological examination revealed mild dysarthria, dysphagia, bilateral ptosis, bilateral hypoacusis, postural tremor, left-sided dysdiadochokinesia, bilateral hip extension weakness (MRC M5-), reduced upper-limb and absent lower-limb deep tendon reflexes, diffuse muscle wasting, bilateral stocking-type sensory loss, and ataxic stance (ambulatory with a walker).
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed marked leukocytosis peaking at 38.8/nL on hospital day (hd) 3 (reference: 4.0-9.0/nL), severe thrombocytopenia nadir of 4/nL on hd 15 and 18 (reference: 150-450/nL), renal insufficiency, elevated CRP peaking at 34.7 mg/dL on hd 3 (reference: <=0.6 mg/dL), elevated AST (GOT), ALT (GPT), and LDH, normal creatine kinase, mild hypocalcemia, elevated ferritin 3,817 ng/mL (reference: 30-400 ng/mL), hyperthyroid parameters, and HbA1c 7.4% (reference: <=6%). Chest X-ray showed bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates up to 1 cm (predominantly left lower lobe), a horizontal interlobar pleural effusion, and an encapsulated right diagonal interlobar effusion (compared with a normal CXR 5 weeks prior).
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT revealed an 11 x 7 cm contrast-enhancing mass in the right upper lobe with central and peripheral necrosis plus bilateral irregular hyperdensities. Brain MRI demonstrated a 4-mm hyperintense enhancing lesion in the superior cerebellar vermis and bilateral small occipital deep white matter and subcortical hyperintensities. Lumbar puncture was contraindicated due to severe thrombocytopenia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated (pulmonary and cerebral) nocardiosis caused by Nocardia sp. in an immunocompromised splenectomized patient on chronic corticosteroids was confirmed via sputum cultures growing Nocardia sp. After initial empirical amoxicillin (hd 2-4), caspofungin (hd 4-7), and piperacillin (hd 5-7), he was treated with intravenous meropenem from hd 8 to hd 45 (while phenprocoumon was stopped and prednisolone/danazol were adjusted for severe ITP) and discharged on long-term oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. At 3-month follow-up, pulmonary lesions had regressed but cerebral lesions progressed despite TMP-SMX, prompting switches to sultamicillin and then meropenem; he died shortly thereafter of an acute myocardial infarction, with autopsy excluding pulmonary malignancy and confirming persistent cerebral infection despite negative post-mortem brain tissue cultures.
